newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli shares close lower after CPI upset.
newsitem.headline: Israeli shares close lower after CPI upset.

text.p: Israeli shares closed broadly lower on Wednesday following the release of an unexpectedly high June consumer price index, traders said.
The benchmark Mishtanim index of the top 100 shares fell 1.20 percent, or 3.60 points, to 295.80 on a low all-share turnover of 130 million shekels against 134 million on Tuesday.
The Maof 25 blue chip index closed 0.86 percent lower at 303.32.
The June CPI, released on Tuesday after the end of trading, rose 1.1 percent, well above expectations of a rise of 0.5-0.8 percent.
"We were expecting a sharper decline following the surprising CPI figure, but the market showed strength," said Michael Weiss at Evergreen Capital Markets.

"At the beginning of the day investors expected that the market would lose as much as two and half percent but in the end there were only a few sellers," said a trader at the First International Bank of Israel (FIBI).
"I believe that the central bank will leave its key lending rate unchanged at the end of the month," Weiss said.

The FIBI trader said most analysts believed the June inflation index did not point to accelerating inflation. "The figure was affected by the sharp depreciation of the shekel. In the long run inflation will continue to decline," he said.
The Israeli shekel has dropped about 4.5 percent since the government announced changes in the exchange rate mechanism and the Bank of Israel slashed interest rates in mid-June.
Weiss added that the mood in the market was still positive but it was hard to predict where the market was going.

"Share prices are reasonable now, but the alternatives are becoming less attractive as bond yields are continuing to fall. It's hard to say what will happen in the near term, but the mood in the market is very optimistic," he said.

The FIBI trader said the fact that shares had been falling on low volume indicated that the trend was still positive. "There is no panic and investors are not rushing to sell. Most players believe that the market is still positive."
However, the market would remain at its current level until the expiry of Maof July options at the end of the month. "After the expiry the market will resume its rise," he said.

Lehman Brothers initiated coverage of Dead Sea Bromine with a 2-outperform rating, saying the company was set to experience strong sustainable growth from new business activities. It said Bromine would earn $0.41 a share in 1997 and $0.50 in 1998 against $0.36 in 1996.
Dead Sea lost 0.25 percent to 1,108 agorot.

The most active shares were Teva Pharmaceutical Industries, which fell 1.75 percent to 22,143 agorot on volume of 7.8 million shekels; Bezeq Israel Telecom, which fell 0.25 percent to 1,061 agorot on volume of 6.7 million shekels; and Bank Leumi, which lost 1.0 percent to 568 agorot on turnover of 5.7 million shekels.
- Dan Gerstenfeld, Tel Aviv newsroom, 972-3-537-2211 x233
